<reason>CON built a persistent, largely unrebutted objection: opt-in does nothing for the person who doesn't yet know a topic exists, since a toggle only helps someone who already knows to flip it — a point raised in the opening (A1.4-1.5), sharpened in Rebuttal 1 (A2.5-2.6), honestly conceded-but-reframed under pressure (A4.3), and driven home in the closing (A5.4). PRO's answer never moved past "it only costs one click," which concedes rather than answers the discovery problem. CON also used its pressure question about the worker's safety-reform video to expose a real mismatch in PRO's topic-based rule: PRO's own answer (B4.1) that "asking for legal reform" is itself the trigger for gating conceded that the rule targets subject matter rather than manipulation, and CON's closing crystallized this cleanly ("the grievance can be furious; the proposed remedy can be calm. The rule distinguishes neither"). PRO's strongest counter — that its binary opt-in is externally checkable while CON's "reweighting" is an unauditable internal promise — was a good point, but CON blunted it by showing PRO's own topic classification requires just as much boundary-drawing (the reform-call edge case), and by disciplined hedging rather than overclaiming ("I have not established... my argument does not require that claim"). Both sides executed the Q&A format correctly, but CON's answers did more actual work resolving the live pressure, while PRO's answers tended to accept the cost and re-assert the click-based framing rather than dissolve the discovery objection.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The worker's-safety-video exchange: CON's pressure question (A3.1) forced PRO to admit a reform-framed grievance gets gated as "political" (B4.1: "that's a feature, not a flaw"), and CON's closing turned that concession into the decisive flaw — the rule filters the move from grievance to public remedy, not actual manipulation.</best_rebuttal>
